title: SDK cheat sheet: streaming tool surface patterns for TS/Py/Go
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Purpose:
Create a compact, copy-ready engineering ticket that defines a minimal, consistent SDK surface for streaming responses, tool/function callbacks, and typed/structured result envelopes across TypeScript, Python, and Go. This is intended to be a practical cheat-sheet + reference implementations package that SDK authors can use to ensure compatibility with the core API streaming and tool-calling primitives without carrying the full legacy adapter complexity.

Context and motivation:
- Teams keep re-implementing similar adapter code for each language when wiring streaming + tool callbacks. This results in subtle behavioral drift (ordering, error propagation, partial outputs) and brittle user examples.
- Core API supports incremental event streams, tool invocation frames, and structured JSON envelopes. We need canonical, small-footprint patterns that emphasize predictable ordering, backpressure-friendly consumption, and clear error semantics.
- This work should reduce customer-reported integration bugs and speed up onboarding examples in our docs and Quickstarts.

Scope (what this ticket will deliver):
1) A single-page "cheat sheet" describing the canonical event envelope and ordering guarantees we expect SDKs to preserve.
2) Minimal reference implementations (approx ~60-120 LOC each) for TypeScript, Python, and Go that:  - stream the core event types to a consumer API (onEvent/onComplete/onError)  - expose a lightweight tool invocation callback surface (registerTool(name, handler))  - emit typed structured outputs (result.envelope with version and schema metadata)  - demonstrate a pattern for resuming/continuing partially-received outputs (cursor semantics)
3) Clear acceptance criteria and test cases linking to unit/integration tests and a demo app used by the docs team.

Design constraints and trade-offs:
- Keep the surface intentionally small: one streaming iterator/observable and one tool registry API per language. Avoid adding multiple competing abstractions.
- Favor explicit framing rather than trying to derive structure from freeform tokens (helps deterministic parsing across runtimes).
- Use a compact envelope with fields: "type", "seq", "payload", "schema_version". This minimizes runtime coupling while enabling schema evolution.
- Backpressure: the reference patterns should not block runtime event pumps; instead they provide an async pull/consume API and an optional internal buffer with a configurable size.
- Error handling: introduce canonical error frames (type=error) with machine-readable code and human message. SDKs should surface both structured error and underlying transport error where available.

Compatibility matrix (high-level):
- TypeScript: Node 18+, Deno (later PR), Browser streaming via ReadableStream examples
- Python: 3.10+ async iterator + synchronous helper for legacy code paths
- Go: 1.20+ context-aware channel pattern with Cancel semantics

Deliverables (artifacts):
- cheat_sheet.md (single-page reference for SDK authors and docs)
- ts/reference_streaming_tool.ts (compact example, ~80 LOC)
- py/reference_streaming_tool.py (compact example, ~90 LOC)
- go/reference_streaming_tool.go (compact example, ~110 LOC)
- unit tests for each language demonstrating ordering, error propagation, and schema validation
- docs PR linking Quickstart snippets to the new examples

Acceptance Criteria:
- [ ] Cheat sheet reviewed and accepted by SDK lead and API design (comments resolved)
- [ ] TypeScript example passes CI and demonstrates: streaming events -> consumption order preserved; tool invocation round-trip; structured result with schema_version
- [ ] Python example passes CI and demonstrates the same behaviors (both async and sync helper)
- [ ] Go example passes CI and demonstrates context cancellation and error frames
- [ ] Test matrix covers at least: partial output resumption, tool handler exception propagation, invalid-schema rejection, and backpressure limit enforcement
- [ ] Docs Quickstart PR references the three examples and lands at least one runnable snippet for Node and Python

Notes on example behavior (for reviewers):
- Envelope example (stringified JSON per-frame) we will use in examples: {
  "type": "event|tool|complete|error",
  "seq": <monotonic int>,
  "payload": {...},
  "schema_version": "1.0"
}
- Ordering: seq values guarantee causal order for frames emitted from the same invocation. Parallel tool invocations interleave but each tool's frames keep increasing sequences with tool id namespace included in payload when needed.
- Tool callbacks are first-class: SDK exposes a small registry with typed handler signatures. Handler returns either immediate structured result or an async stream producer. SDK will never swallow handler exceptions; it must emit an error frame with handler stack/summary and a machine code mapping.

Risks and mitigation:
- Risk: Examples get treated as the canonical API rather than a minimal pattern and SDK teams feel constrained. Mitigation: Emphasize these are intentionally minimal reference patterns; provide extension points in cheat sheet.
- Risk: Too many language-specific edge cases. Mitigation: keep canonical semantics language-agnostic and push language ergonomics into thin wrapper helpers (not the core contract).

Next steps / plan for the sprint:
- Week 1: Draft cheat sheet + TypeScript reference implementation + unit tests
- Week 2: Python and Go references + tests; initial docs PR with Node snippet
- Week 3: Address review feedback, polish examples for quickstarts, land SDK lead sign-off and close ticket
acceptance_criteria: Cheat sheet approved; TS/Py/Go ref implementations pass CI and demonstrate ordering, tool round-trips, partial resumption, error frames and schema_version in envelopes; docs PR links examples
